title: The friendliest verbs
goal: Use the easiest and biggest verb group (*-am / -asz*), then build questions with *czy* and question words.
bekal: conjugate *-am / -asz* verbs for all six persons without thinking
make yes/no questions with *czy* — and know when it can be dropped
use eight question words that cover almost every beginner conversation

dialogs.title: Dialogue — W bibliotece
dialogs.intro: The campus library, midday. Budi sits with a newspaper open and a puzzled look.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Czytam gazetę. Ale nie rozumiem wszystkiego.
lines.id: I'm reading the paper. But I don't understand everything.
lines.literal: I-read newspaper. but not I-understand everything.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: To normalne. Ja też czytam po angielsku bardzo powoli.
lines.id: That's normal. I read English very slowly too.
lines.literal: that normal. I also read in-English very slowly.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Do you listen to the radio in Polish?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Codziennie rano. A ty? Oglądasz polskie filmy?
lines.id: Every morning. And you? Do you watch Polish films?
lines.literal: every-day morning. and you? you-watch Polish films?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I do, but I understand maybe half.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mam słownik w telefonie. Pytam też kolegów.
lines.id: I have a dictionary on my phone. I ask my friends too.
lines.literal: I-have dictionary in phone. I-ask also friends.

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Znasz aplikację Lingo? Wszyscy studenci jej używają.
lines.id: Do you know the Lingo app? All the students use it.
lines.literal: you-know app Lingo? all students it use.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: No, I don't. How does it work?

lines.speaker: Ania:
lines.text: Pokażę ci jutro. Czekam na ciebie o piątej.
lines.id: I'll show you tomorrow. I'll wait for you at five.
lines.literal: I-will-show to-you tomorrow. I-wait on you at fifth.

notes: **This group is the friendliest**, and a big win for beginners: it has the most members, the most regular endings, and not a single letter in the stem changes. *Czytać → czytam, czytasz, czyta…* — just drop *-ć* and add the ending.

**Czy** is a spoken question mark. It stands at the **start of the sentence** and turns a statement into a yes/no question without changing the word order at all: *Słuchasz radia* (you listen to the radio) → *Czy słuchasz radia?* (do you listen to the radio?).
**And it can be dropped.** In conversation, *Masz słownik?* with rising intonation is just as correct and heard more often — like English "You have a dictionary?".

**Rozumieć misbehaves a little.** Its forms are *rozumiem, rozumiesz, rozumie, rozumiemy, rozumiecie, rozumieją* — the *ja* and *my* endings match this group, but the *oni* ending is *-eją*. Learn it as it is; it's too common to skip.

**Gazetę, aplikację, połowę** — all end in *-ę*. That's no accident: a feminine noun that is the **object** of an action gets the ending *-ę*. This form is called *biernik* and is the whole topic of Unit 7. For now, just notice the pattern in passing.
**Kolegów** isn't the dictionary form either, and it isn't *biernik* — nouns for **male people** behave differently again. Don't worry: they're introduced gradually from Unit 7.

**Czekam na ciebie** — "I wait **on** you". Polish requires the preposition *na* after *czekać*, where English uses "for". Verbs that come with a fixed preposition like this are best learned as a package: *czekać na*, *pytać o*, *dziękować za*.
**Wszyscy studenci** — the plural for a group that includes men. Compare *wszystkie studentki* for a group of women. The pattern you met with *ci / te* in Unit 3 is back again.

grammars.title: Group III: -am / -asz
body: Drop *-ć* from the dictionary form, then add these six endings. No other letter changes.
after: Look at the **on / ona / ono** form: its ending is just *-a*, the shortest of all. This holds throughout Polish — the "he/she" form is always the shortest, and the "ja" form always ends in *-m*.

*Mieć* (to have) belongs to this group even though its dictionary form is short: *mam, masz, ma, mamy, macie, mają*. It's one of the verbs you'll use most, so practice it until it comes out without thinking.
⚠️ Don't add pronouns unless you really want emphasis. *Czytam gazetę* is already complete; *Ja czytam gazetę* means "**I'm** the one reading the paper".

grammars.title: Asking questions in Polish
body: Two kinds of questions, and both are simpler than in English — there's no helper word like *do/does* to slot in.

head: Type
How to make it
Example
rows: add *czy* at the front, or just raise your voice
question word first, the rest stays

after: ⚠️ Don't confuse *czy* and *jak*. The test: *czy* expects the answer **tak** or **nie**; *jak* expects an explanation.
Negating is just as easy: put *nie* right before the verb. *Nie czytam.* *Nie mam czasu.* *Nie rozumiem.* No helper word, no change in word order.

blocks.text: They all behave exactly the same. If you know *czytam*, you can already use all fourteen.

head: Dictionary form
ja

Meaning
rows: to come back, to go home

blocks.title: Three sentences you can use right away
items: *Nie pamiętam.* — I don't remember. (used ten times a day by beginners)
*Szukam ulicy Długiej.* — I'm looking for Długa Street.
*Kocham polską kuchnię.* — I love Polish cooking.

blocks.text: A short answer in Polish repeats the verb itself instead of using a helper like "yes, I do".
Look at the last column: *nie* appears **twice** — once as the answer "no", once to negate the verb. That's correct and required; dropping either one sounds lopsided.

blocks.title: If you didn't catch the question
items: *Słucham?* — "Sorry?" (literally "I'm listening?") Also used when answering the phone.
*Nie wiem, jak to powiedzieć.* — I don't know how to say it.

vocab.en: to go home; to come back
